title: Anarchy, Chokepoints, and the Bargaining Range: Structural Realism vs. Liberal Institutionalism & Constructivism in International Relations — Why rational states fight ruinous wars when peaceful bargains exist; Mearsheimer's 1994 offensive-realist assault on institutions vs Keohane's 1998 transaction-cost & shadow-of-the-future defense; Wendt's 1992 Hobbesian-Lockean-Kantian anarchy & Oneal-Russett's 1885-1992 Kantian triad MID regressions; Fearon's 1995 private-information & commitment-problem theorem; Copeland's 1996 future-trade cutoff switch & Farrell-Newman's 2019 SWIFT/semiconductor panopticon & chokepoint coercion; preventive-war discount math, dyadic IV power & spotting IR paradigms in disguise

teenKit.tldr: International politics is a high-stakes survival game played without a global police force, forcing sovereign states to constantly suspect each other even when peace is mathematically cheaper than war.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It explains why global superpowers can be trapped into devastating conflicts by simple fear of what the other might do tomorrow, much like two people in a dark room both holding loaded weapons.
keyTakeaways: Anarchy in global politics does not mean street chaos; it simply means there is no supreme world government or 911 to protect countries from invasion.
Rationalist bargaining theory proves that war is a costly mistake caused by hidden information, pride, or the inability to trust future promises.
Modern global networks like SWIFT financial clearinghouses and semiconductor supply chains mean countries can use everyday trade hubs as weapons of mass economic coercion.

vocab.meaning: The total absence of a central global government or world police force capable of enforcing laws or protecting sovereign states.
The theory that because the world is anarchic, great powers are forced to obsess over military power and survival above all else.
A deadly trap where two sides cannot agree to a peaceful deal today because neither can guarantee the other won't attack tomorrow once they get stronger.
The modern strategy where powerful nations use their control over global economic hubs, like the internet or banking networks, to spy on and bully rivals.

quiz.question: What does the term 'anarchy' specifically mean in the study of international relations?
options: Riots and lawless chaos breaking out inside major cities
The complete absence of a higher global authority or world police
A political system run exclusively by radical anti-government rebels
The total collapse of international trade and stock markets
quiz.explanation: In political science, anarchy simply means there is no global government sitting above sovereign nations to enforce rules.

quiz.question: According to James Fearon's 1995 bargaining theorem, why do rational states sometimes end up fighting ruinous wars?
options: Because human leaders are always completely irrational and emotionally unstable
Because countries actually prefer losing money and lives over peaceful compromises
Because hidden information and commitment problems prevent them from trusting peaceful deals
Because international organizations like the United Nations force nations to fight
quiz.explanation: Fearon proved that rational states fight because they hide their true capabilities or cannot trust that the other side will keep a promise in the future.

quiz.question: What is 'weaponized interdependence' as discovered by Farrell and Newman in 2019?
options: Using global supply chain hubs and financial networks as choke points to coerce rivals
Forcing all countries to use the exact same currency to prevent military conflict
Building massive physical walls around democratic nations to stop economic trade
A military alliance where countries share their nuclear weapons codes
quiz.explanation: Weaponized interdependence happens when dominant nodes in global networks, like SWIFT banking, are used as political weapons to monitor and punish adversaries.
